items.answer:
(a) Ventricles have thicker muscular walls than atria because they have to pump blood into various organs of the body.
(b) The transport system in plants is slow because: (i) plants have low energy needs, (ii) plant bodies have a large proportion of dead cells in many tissues, and (iii) plants do not move.
(c) Aquatic vertebrates like fish have a two-chambered heart (one atrium and one ventricle). The heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the gills, where it gets oxygenated, and the oxygenated blood from the gills is supplied to the body parts. Thus blood goes only once through the heart during one cycle of passage through the body. In terrestrial organisms the heart may be three or four chambered, blood gets oxygenated in the lungs and most of them have double circulation.
(d) The water column in the xylem tracheids and vessels moves upwards due to the pull generated by transpiration (loss of water in the form of vapour from the living tissues of the aerial parts of the plant). Water is lost through the tiny pores called stomata present on the surface of the leaves. Stomata are open during the daytime, so transpiration is faster and water along with minerals moves faster through the xylem during the day as compared to the night.
(e) Veins have valves that ensure that the blood flows only in one direction. The valves allow blood to flow only towards the heart and prevent back-flow, but arteries do not have valves.

items.stem: How would you classify a green plant, an animal, a fungus and a roundworm based on their modes of nutrition? Explain very briefly the manner how they get their nutrition.
items.answer:
A green plant is an autotroph, which produces its own food by photosynthesis, using CO₂ and water as raw materials (obtained from the atmosphere and the soil) and using sunlight.

items.stem: What are the various steps involved in the holozoic mode of nutrition?
items.answer:
The different steps of the holozoic mode of nutrition are (i) Ingestion (ii) Digestion (iii) Absorption (iv) Assimilation (v) Egestion.
Ingestion is the taking in of food into the body or alimentary canal. Amoeba engulfs the food by forming pseudopodia all around it and captures the food into a food vacuole; this is called phagocytosis.
Digestion is the breaking down of complex and insoluble food with the help of enzymes into simpler and soluble substances so that they can be utilised in the body. In Amoeba digestion occurs in the food vacuole with the help of digestive enzymes.
Absorption is the diffusion of the digested food into the cytoplasm.
Assimilation is the utilisation of the digested food by the cell.
Egestion is the removal or throwing out of the undigested food from the body.

items.stem: Why is respiration important for all living organisms?

Respiration is important for all living organisms because:

(ii) For the removal of toxic carbon dioxide: carbon dioxide is produced in our tissues as a result of the oxidation of food. items.stem: Explain the mechanism of breathing.
items.answer:
For continued gaseous exchange in the lungs a constant renewal of air is necessary. This happens in two steps.
(i) Inspiration (inhalation), i.e. drawing air into the lungs, is the result of an increase in the size of the thoracic cavity due to the combined action of the ribs and the diaphragm. The ribs are moved upward and outward by the intercostal muscles, enlarging the chest cavity all around. The diaphragm, a sheet of muscular tissue normally arched upward like a dome towards the base of the lungs, contracts and flattens to an almost horizontal plane, enlarging the chest cavity lengthwise. As the chest cavity increases in size the pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, so outside air rushes in to equalise the pressure.
(ii) Expiration (exhalation), i.e. expelling air out, is the result of the reverse movements of the ribs and the diaphragm. The other set of intercostal muscles contracts and pulls the ribs down and inward, and the diaphragm relaxes and moves upward to its dome-like outline under the pressure of the abdominal contents. The cavity of the thorax is diminished, the lungs are compressed and the air is forced out into the atmosphere.

items.stem: What is transpiration? Mention its importance to the plants.
items.answer:
Transpiration is the loss of water in the form of water vapour from the surface of the leaf (and other aerial parts of the plant) into the atmosphere.
Transpiration has great significance for plants. Its main advantages are as follows:
1. Cooling effect: Evaporation reduces temperature. Therefore transpiration is useful to plants on hot sunny days.
2. Suction force: Transpiration helps in the ascent of sap by producing a suction force acting from the top of the plant. Evaporation from the leaves concentrates the cell sap and increases its osmotic pressure. This draws water from the cells of the lower levels in a sequential manner (ascent of sap) and finally favours absorption of water from the soil by osmosis.
3. Distribution of water: Since leaves are present at the tips of all branches and twigs, transpiration from their surfaces tends to draw water towards them and thus helps in the distribution of water throughout the plant body.
4. Elimination of excess water: Roots continuously absorb a very large quantity of water. Transpiration is an effective method of removing excess water from the plant body.

items.stem: What is translocation? Name the cells involved in the transport of food in plants. What are the steps involved in the translocation of food in plants?
items.answer:
Transportation of the soluble products of photosynthesis (food) from the leaves to other parts of the plant is called translocation.
The sieve tubes of phloem are the cells involved in the transport of food in plants.
For translocation, food molecules enter into the sieve tubes, from where they can be transported upwards or downwards to all parts of the plant including the roots. The mechanism of translocation is an active process that utilises energy. Materials are transferred from the leaf cells, or from the site of storage, into the phloem tissue. Energy is required for this and is provided by ATP molecules. This energy increases the osmotic pressure, as a result of which water from outside moves into the phloem. This pressure maintains the movement of food through all the parts of the plant.

items.stem:
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) is a condition characterized by a gradual loss of kidney function over time. CKD is also known as chronic renal disease. With increasing life expectancy and prevalence of life style diseases, US has seen a 30% increase in prevalence of Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD) in the last decade. Unfortunately, from India there is no longitudinal study and limited data on the prevalence of CKD. In western countries, diabetes and hypertension account for over 2/3rd of the cases of CKD. In India too, diabetes and hypertension today account for 40-60% cases of CKD. As per recent Indian Council of Medical Research data, prevalence of diabetes in Indian adult population has risen to 7.1% (varying from 5.8% in Jharkhand to 13.5% in Chandigarh) and in urban population (over the age of 40 years) the prevalence is as high as 28%. Likewise, the reported prevalence of hypertension in the adult population today is 17% (14.8% from rural and 21.4% from urban belt). A similar prevalence of 17.4% has been reported by Panesar et al. (in the age group of 20-59 years) even from a slum-resettlement colony of Delhi. With rising prevalence of these diseases in India, prevalence of CKD is expected to rise and obviously, this is the key target population to address. A study published in this issue is from a rural belt of Karnataka. The population had a mean age of 39.88 ± 15.87 years with 3.82% prevalence of diabetes and 33.62% of hypertension. Authors found 6.3% prevalence of CKD stage 3, which is the highest reported till date by any Indian worker. It is disturbing to note the high prevalence of hypertension in a rural setting where over 75% population had normal or low body mass index. In comparison to most other published studies from India, the present study population is younger and even the prevalence of diabetes is low, but surprisingly despite that the prevalence of stage 3 CKD is reported to be higher (6.3%). It is disturbing to see the rising prevalence of hypertension and CKD in rural belts. Possibly, with shifting population the difference between urban and rural areas is getting blurred. Undoubtedly, we need more Indian data to validate these findings.

(i) What is CKD?
(ii) What are the major causes of CKD?
(iii) In which segment of society is CKD more prevalent?
(iv) What is the highest percentage of CKD reported?
items.answer:
(i) CKD is a condition characterized by a gradual loss of kidney function over time.
(ii) Diabetes and hypertension.
(iii) Rural (the highest reported prevalence comes from a rural belt).
(iv) 6.3% (prevalence of CKD stage 3).

items.stem:
The leaf is the main photosynthetic organ in a plant. It controls gas exchange in plants and controls the amount of water loss in plants. Upper epidermis cells contain no chloroplasts, which is not true for the guard cells. They form layers on the upper and lower surface of the leaf. Their function is to prevent water from getting out and to stop unwanted substances/organisms getting in. The palisade mesophyll layer is where most of the photosynthesis occurs in the leaf. The palisade cells contain a lot of chloroplasts to help them perform this photosynthesis. Lower epidermis is the bottom layer of the leaf and is one cell thick. It may not contain a cuticle; within the lower epidermis, there are some holes found in leaves called stoma. These holes allow gases to diffuse in and out of the leaves. The stoma are formed by two highly specialized epidermis cells, called guard cells. Guard cells are the only epidermis cells that contain chloroplasts.

(i) Mention two functions of lower epidermis.
(ii) Where are chloroplasts present in the leaf?
(iii) What are the functions of xylem and phloem in leaf?
(iv) List one structural and one functional difference between upper and lower epidermis.
items.answer:
(i) (a) To allow transpiration. (b) To allow gas exchange.
(ii) In the guard cells and the palisade cells.
(iii) Xylem: it transports water and minerals to the leaf cells. Phloem: it translocates the dissolved food prepared by photosynthesis in the palisade cells.
(iv) Structural difference: the upper epidermis has a cuticle and does not have stomata, or has fewer stomata; the lower epidermis may not have a cuticle and has more stomata. Functional difference: the upper epidermis is more for protection while the lower epidermis is for gas exchange and transpiration.
